Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Banking and Finance CIB Ghana’s 3rd post-MPC Policy seminar focuses on monetary policy transmission, credit growth 20 October 2026 7:53am Audio By Carbonatix
… Bank of Ghana, Ministry of Finance, banks, traders and industry examine why cheaper money is reaching some borrowers faster than others
Lower interest rates are reaching borrowers of Ghana’s universal banks faster than customers of community and microfinance banks, according to a survey of banks presented at the third Post-Monetary Policy Committee (Post-MPC) Policy Seminar of Chartered Institute of Bankers, Ghana (CIB Ghana).
The seminar, held at the CIB Ghana Auditorium and streamed on the Institute’s social media platforms, brought together the Bank of Ghana (BoG), the Ministry of Finance, banks, traders and industry. Discussions centered on monetary policy transmission, credit growth and non-performing loans (NPLs).It followed the 132nd meeting of the BoG’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which voted unanimously on 24 September to keep the policy rate unchanged at 14.0 percent.
Opening the seminar, the President of CIB Ghana Governing Council, Dr. Mrs. Ellen Ohene-Afoakwa, FCIB, said monetary policy had implications beyond economists and central bankers, as its effects were transmitted through financial markets, lending conditions, businesses and households. She said that the effectiveness of monetary policy depended not only on changes in the policy rate but also on the extent to which those changes were transmitted to the wider economy.“ As an institute, we recognise that credit growth and credit quality must move together,” she said.
She added that Ghana needed a banking sector capable of providing adequate credit to productive sectors while maintaining strong risk management and responsible lending practices. On NPLs, she said greater attention should be placed on preventing bad loans than on recovering them after they had deteriorated.
In remarks read on his behalf by the BoG’s Director of Research, Dr. Simon Harvey, the Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr. Johnson P. Asiama, said changes in the policy rate do not pass through to borrowers at once, because banks also weigh funding costs, credit risk, operating costs and expected losses when pricing loans.
“This transmission is neither automatic nor instantaneous,” the Governor said.
He said the aim of monetary policy was not simply to achieve lower interest rates but to maintain anchored inflation expectations, a stable currency and sound financial institutions. He also called for a stronger focus on preventing NPLs. “The objective is not simply to achieve lower interest rates,” he said.
The Governor said the MPC found CIB Ghana’s Pre-MPC survey, which is presented to the Committee ahead of each meeting, insightful, helpful and complementary to its own analytical models.
The Chief Executive Officer of CIB Ghana, Mr. Robert Dzato, FCIB, presented findings from the Institute’s September Pre-MPC sentiment survey, which the CIB Ghana research team conducts among banks ahead of each MPC meeting to gather industry insights to support the work of the MPC. Mr. Dzato said the survey showed strong appetite among banks to lend, although the impact of monetary policy transmission varied across market segments. “ We see appetite to lend is quite high,” he said, noting that “the real impact of the transmission of monetary policy varies across the various segments.”
Lending rates differed widely by type of bank. Most universal banks surveyed reported lending at 10 to 15 percent. Among community banks, 46 percent reported lending at 21 to 25 percent, up from 36 percent in the July survey, while microfinance banks reported rates of roughly 31 to 40 percent.
Although most banks were confident about the wider economy, a majority expected inflation to rise in the coming months, an upside risk that also featured in the panel’s discussion of the MPC’s decision to hold. On asset quality, he described banks’ confidence in meeting the NPL target of 10 percent by year end, as encouraging but warned that faster credit growth had to be matched by stronger monitoring, recovery and risk mitigation. “We are driving credit growth for obvious reasons,” Mr. Dzato said, adding that loans that were not repaid on time could create another problem for the sector.
The panel was moderated by Mrs. Ellen Gyamera, ACIB, Head of the Petroleum Fund at the BoG, and comprised Dr. Simon Harvey, Director of Research of Bank of Ghana; Mr Frederick Amissah, a Technical Advisor to the Ministry of Finance; Dr. Charles Atuahene, Executive Member of Finance and Administration Committee of Association of Ghana Industries (AGI); Mr. John Awuah, Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Association of Banks and Mr. Clement Boateng, the President of the Ghana Union of Traders Association (GUTA).
Dr. Harvey set out the basis for the MPC’s decision to hold the policy rate, including upside risks to inflation. Mr. Amissah spoke on coordination between fiscal and monetary authorities, and on the role of fiscal discipline in keeping prices stable and bringing down government borrowing costs. Panellists noted that loan pricing had fallen from its past highs and discussed the scope for further declines over time. Mr. Awuah addressed access to credit, the documentation and record-keeping borrowers need to qualify, and the role of collateral enforcement and the courts in recovering bad loans, drawing comparisons with NPL levels elsewhere in the region.
Mr. Boateng called for repayment terms, including grace periods, that reflect traders’ import cycles and shipping delays. Dr. Atuahene discussed how exchange rate movements affect exporters’ competitiveness, input costs and businesses’ appetite to borrow.
Dr. Ohene-Afoakwa highlighted the Institute’s growth in professional education, certification and ethics, including its Non-Interest Banking Certification, Branch CEO Programme, digital and ESG certifications and Ethics 2.0 class. She also noted Ghana’s success in winning the right to host the World Conference of Banking Institutes in 2028. She also appealed for support for the Institute’s planned modern bankers’ house and business complex, describing the project as an investment in the future of the banking profession and in building a stronger, more professional and future-ready financial sector. The seminar forms part of events leading up to the annual Bankers Week.
